# Softland Imported Topology View — Design Research Report

## TL;DR
- The Imported Topology View should be designed as an **orientation instrument, not a dashboard**: a three-pane "navigator + topology browser + provenance inspector" layout governed by Shneiderman's "overview first, zoom and filter, then details on demand," where the default representations are lists and outlines and graphs appear only as *locally-scoped, depth-limited neighborhoods* — never an all-world hairball.
- The deepest design lineage (Bush's trails, Engelbart's ViewSpecs, Nelson's transclusion, Kay/Reenskaug's one-model-many-views, Bret Victor's "no hidden state," Ink & Switch's lenses) converges on three transferable imperatives for Softland: **make provenance visible and bidirectional, treat views as projections over shared objects, and never hide the path back to raw source.**
- The strongest production precedents to borrow concretely are **source maps** (native→raw anchoring), **VS Code Peek** (inspect-without-losing-place), **DataHub lineage** (expand-one-hop, blast-radius, health badges), **Figma's selection-driven inspector**, **Obsidian's local-graph depth slider**, and **Notion's views-over-one-database** — each solving an orientation/trust problem Softland shares.

## Key Findings

1. **The canonical interaction grammar is already settled.** Ben Shneiderman's Visual Information-Seeking Mantra — "Overview first, zoom and filter, then details-on-demand" — comes from "The Eyes Have It: A Task by Data Type Taxonomy for Information Visualizations" (Proc. 1996 IEEE Symposium on Visual Languages, pp. 336–343; DOI 10.1109/VL.1996.545307), now cited roughly 5,700 times per Semantic Scholar, making it among the most-cited organizing principles in information visualization. It maps almost perfectly onto the orientation-first goal of the Imported Topology View. The mantra exists because overview gives context, filtering isolates significant structure, and details-on-demand prevents screen clutter; the empirical grounding came from Shneiderman's FilmFinder/starfield work.

2. **Provenance must be bidirectional and visible — this is the throughline of the entire tools-for-thought canon.** Bush's Memex made *trails* (associative links) first-class objects to be saved, named, and shared; Nelson's Xanadu insisted on two-way links and transclusion so "it is possible to see the origins of every quotation"; Engelbart's NLS used bidirectional links and ViewSpecs. Softland's SourceAnchor and CompositionEdge are direct descendants of this lineage and must be rendered, not merely stored.

3. **"Views are projections over shared objects" is a 45-year-old, validated pattern.** Trygve Reenskaug formulated Model-View-Controller at Xerox PARC in 1978–79; in his own MVC notes he states: "The essential purpose of MVC is to bridge the gap between the human user's mental model and the digital model that exists in the computer… The structure is useful if the user needs to see the same model element simultaneously in different contexts and/or from different viewpoints." Notion/Coda's "views over one database" is the modern mass-market proof. Softland's Projection/View concept should be implemented as true projections (filters/sorts/layouts over the same ObjectContainers), never copies.

4. **Graphs are useful only when locally scoped and depth-limited; global graphs reliably become useless "hairballs."** Obsidian community consensus (per a Code Culture review of r/ObsidianMD) is that the graph "renders cleanly under 50 notes," "starts to degrade" past ~200, and is "reliably a hairball" by ~500 — "visually impressive and navigationally useless." This is backed by the academic hairball literature (edge bundling, clustering, edge-cutting, Furnas's degree-of-interest filtering). Softland must default to local neighborhoods.

5. **The source-map pattern is a near-exact precedent for SourceAnchor.** Source maps map minified/compiled code back to original source positions (file, line, column) via the V3 spec, so developers can — in the verified phrasing of OneUptime's source-maps guide — "debug the code you wrote, not the code that runs." This is structurally identical to Softland's need to map a DerivedUnit/ObjectContainer back to an exact SourceArtifact span — and the affordance is trusted because the mapping is exact, reversible, and always one click away.

## Details

### Part A — Tools-for-Thought Lineage (the "why" that transfers to Softland)

**Vannevar Bush, "As We May Think" (1945) — Memex and associative trails.** Bush's central design argument was that human memory works "by association" and that mechanical indexing fights the grain of the mind. His solution, the *trail*, let a user "tie two items together" permanently and — crucially — name, save, and share that trail; he even foresaw "wholly new forms of encyclopedias… with a mesh of associative trails running through them." The rationale that transfers: in Softland, the *connections themselves* (CompositionEdges, accepted cross-source links) are first-class terrain to be inspected and revisited, not invisible plumbing. Bush also anticipated sharing trails between researchers — the "holding understanding in public form" goal.

**Douglas Engelbart, NLS/Augment, "Augmenting Human Intellect" (1962).** Engelbart built *ViewSpecs* — view specifications that let a user expand/collapse an outline, filter content, or show authorship of sections on the fly, over the same underlying file. The deep rationale was his bootstrapping/co-evolution philosophy: tools and human capability evolve together, so the interface must let the same structure be re-projected for different tasks (editing vs. navigation vs. overview). NLS also pioneered bidirectional links between document nodes. Transfer: Softland's outline/graph/timeline/inspector modes are modern ViewSpecs; the same object must be re-viewable without duplicating it.

**Ted Nelson, Project Xanadu — transclusion, two-way links, deep versioning.** Nelson's xanalogical structure has two orthogonal connection types: *deep links* (connections between things that are different) and *transclusion* (visible, principled re-use showing "the origins and context of quotations"). He explicitly attacked the Web's "fragile ever-breaking one-way links, with no recognition of change or copyright, and no support for multiple versions." Transfer: Softland's preservation of raw SourceArtifact plus SourceAnchors is essentially transclusion-with-provenance; the design must show that a native object is a *manifestation* of preserved source, with the origin visible.

**Alan Kay / Smalltalk — everything is an object, late binding, MVC.** In "The Early History of Smalltalk" (ACM HOPL-II, 1993), Kay grounded Smalltalk in the insight that "everything we can describe can be represented by the recursive composition of a single kind of behavioral building block that hides its combination of state and process inside itself and can be dealt with only through the exchange of messages." Because an object hides its internal representation and exposes behavior, "questions of concrete representation can thus be postponed almost indefinitely" — the philosophical license for one object having many views. From the late-binding perspective Kay describes OOP as "a comprehensive technique for late-binding as many things as possible." His slogan "Doing with Images makes Symbols" (1987 University Video Communications lecture; "User Interface: A Personal View," in Brenda Laurel ed., *The Art of Human-Computer Interface Design*, 1990) borrowed Jerome Bruner's enactive/iconic/symbolic mentalities, mapping doing→mouse/direct-manipulation, images→icons/display, symbols→Smalltalk; the word order matters: "start with the concrete, then use that intuition to expand into the symbolic." It was Trygve Reenskaug who turned this object philosophy into the model/view separation — his original "MODELS – VIEWS – CONTROLLERS" PARC note (10 December 1979) defines "A view is a (visual) representation of its model. It would ordinarily highlight certain attributes of the model and suppress others." Transfer: Softland's ObjectContainer is Kay's object; orientation should start concrete (the raw source, the list) before the abstract (the graph, the schema), and a view should highlight some attributes and fold others.

**Bret Victor — make the invisible visible; no hidden state.** In "Learnable Programming" (2012), Victor's principle: "The system must have no hidden state. State should either be eliminated, or represented as explicit objects on the screen. Every action must have a visible effect." He attacks interfaces where "the entire purpose of code is to manipulate data, and we never see the data. We write with blindfolds." His "Up and Down the Ladder of Abstraction" (2011) argues the deepest insight comes from moving fluidly between concrete and abstract levels. Dynamicland (founded ~2017, shaped with Kay) pushes "tangible programming" where "the spells that power the dynamic behaviour are plainly visible." Transfer: Softland's principles ("provenance must remain inspectable," "raw and native both available," "accepted facts visually distinct from candidates") are direct applications of Victor's no-hidden-state ethic.

**Ink & Switch — local-first, Cambria/lenses, malleable software.** Ink & Switch's Cambria project (Litt, van Hardenberg, et al., 2020) uses *bidirectional lenses* to translate data between schemas, so a document edited in schema B can propagate edits back through the same lens to schema A. Their "Local-first software" essay and the "Malleable software" essay (2025) argue tools should be reshapeable "at the point of use, not through engineering teams at distant corporations." Transfer: Softland's DerivedUnit↔SourceArtifact mapping and Projection/View layer are lens-like; the read-only first view should be built so a later editable/lensed layer is a natural extension, not a rewrite.

**Andy Matuschak & Michael Nielsen — "tools for thought," evergreen notes.** Their essay "How can we develop transformative tools for thought?" (2019) revives the Engelbart/Kay dream and argues notes should be "written and organized to evolve, contribute, and accumulate over time, across projects." Matuschak's evergreen-notes practice ("the goal is not to take notes — the goal is to think effectively"; atomic, concept-oriented notes) is the public-thinking-surface ethos Softland names directly; Nielsen's adjacent work on augmenting cognition and the "mnemonic medium" (Quantum Country) frames understanding as something to be made durable and revisitable. Transfer: the topology view should reward revisiting and handoff — structure visible enough that "another mind can enter without privately reconstructing everything."

**Explorable Explanations (Nicky Case, Distill.pub, Bret Victor).** This movement's design philosophy is that readers learn by inspecting and manipulating models, not just reading. Distill.pub's house style paired interactivity with clarity and visible provenance. Transfer: even a read-only Softland view benefits from inspectability — clicking to reveal the underlying source/relation rather than asserting facts.

**Semantic zoom & ZUIs (Bederson & Hollan, Pad/Pad++/Jazz/Piccolo).** Pad++ distinguished *geometric* zoom (resize) from *semantic* zoom (change representation by scale) — e.g., a clock showing just the hour zoomed out, seconds zoomed in. Most pure ZUIs failed commercially because of disorientation and the cost of free-form spatial navigation, but the surviving idea — *representation changes with scale while identity is preserved* — is exactly Softland's "semantic zoom should preserve identity, provenance, and relations." Transfer: design semantic zoom as discrete, identity-preserving level-of-detail steps (silo → source → object → span), not infinite pan-zoom.

**Furnas's Generalized Fisheye Views / Degree of Interest (1986).** Furnas's DOI function — DOI(x | y) = API(x) − D(x,y), where API is a priori importance and D is distance from the current focus — formalizes *what to show and what to fold*: elements fall below a threshold and are removed from view. His 2006 follow-up emphasizes selection over geometric distortion. Transfer: Softland's "what stays folded vs. visible" should be governed by a degree-of-interest model (importance × distance from the selected object), not arbitrary truncation.

**Provenance visualization research (W3C PROV).** The PROV model's three core classes — Entity, Activity, Agent — with relations (wasGeneratedBy, wasDerivedFrom, wasAttributedTo, used) is the standard vocabulary for "where did this come from," and a provenance graph is formally a directed acyclic graph. Research notes a real usability trap: users misread arrow direction (intuiting data *flow* when the arrow encodes data *dependency*), and "one-size-fits-all" provenance notations confuse domain users. Transfer: Softland should map its substrate to PROV-like semantics (SourceArtifact≈Entity, import/derivation≈Activity, importer/agent≈Agent) but must label edges with plain verbs and disambiguate arrow direction.

### Part B — Production Precedents (concrete patterns + reconstructed rationale)

**Source maps (Chrome DevTools / V3 spec) → SourceAnchor.** The mapping file records, per generated position, the original source file, line, and column (Base64 VLQ-encoded). The reason it earns trust: it is *exact*, *automatic*, and *always one keystroke away* — DevTools shows the original file in the navigator, maps breakpoints and stack traces back, and shows original names in the flame chart, while the browser still runs the minified code. Transfer to SourceAnchor: every native object's inspector must offer a "reveal in source" that opens the exact preserved SourceArtifact span; the affordance is trusted only if it's exact and reversible.

**VS Code / Visual Studio Peek vs. Go to Definition.** Two affordances, deliberately distinct: *Go to Definition* (F12) switches your context to the definition's window; *Peek Definition* (Alt+F12) shows the same information in an inline pop-up "without switching away from the code that you're writing," preserving your place, and supports breadcrumb navigation across nested peeks. The rationale: jumping is disorienting when you only need to *check* something. Transfer: Softland inspection should default to Peek-style overlays (inspect a relation/source without losing your place in the topology browser), with an explicit "jump to" for committed navigation.

**DataHub lineage → topology/graph view.** DataHub renders lineage as an expandable graph centered on a node, where (verbatim from its docs) "the number on the expand lineage button represents how many data-dependence upstreams / downstreams the task has… Note that you can only expand one task's upstreams and one task's downstreams at a time, to keep the visualization simple." It frames impact analysis as "blast radius," shows health/freshness badges on nodes, supports column-level drill-down via breadcrumb, and is search-first for discovery. The reasoning: data estates are far too large to show at once, so the design forces progressive, one-hop expansion from a focus node and uses status encodings to make trust legible at a glance. Transfer: Softland's local graph should expand one hop at a time from the selected object, show edge/relation counts on collapsed nodes, and badge object status (accepted vs. candidate, connected vs. orphan).

**Figma — layers + canvas + inspector triad.** Figma's three detached regions (left navigation/layers, center canvas, right properties/inspector) are selection-driven: selecting on canvas or in the layers panel populates the right inspector, with a solid purple box on the selection and a dashed box on its parent for orientation. Components vs. instances encodes *identity vs. derived copy* (the diamond icon marks a true instance), and hovering a property row highlights the corresponding canvas object with a light purple highlight "so you know what you're editing." Rationale: a stable spatial division of labor (browse / see / inspect) lets power users build muscle memory. Transfer: Softland's three-pane model is the same; the component/instance distinction is a precedent for ObjectContainer (identity) vs. DerivedUnit (derived span), and hover-to-highlight links inspector rows to topology nodes.

**Obsidian / Roam — local vs. global graph, backlinks.** Obsidian explicitly offers a *local* graph with an adjustable **depth** slider (each depth level reveals notes one hop further) plus filters (orphans, tags, attachments) and toggles for incoming vs. outgoing links — and its own community calls the global graph a cluttered "hairball" that "looks fancy… but doesn't serve the purpose." The backlinks/unlinked-mentions panel surfaces relationships textually. Rationale: people work in neighborhoods, not whole vaults. Transfer: this is the direct model for Softland's "avoid giant all-world graph" principle — default to local, depth-limited, with explicit incoming/outgoing distinction.

**Discourse Graphs (Joel Chan et al.) — a named Softland source type.** Discourse Graphs structure research as typed nodes — **Question, Claim, Evidence** — linked by typed relations (*supports*, *opposes*, *informs*). The design rationale (from Chan's "Discourse Graphs for Augmented Knowledge Synthesis" and his knowledge-synthesis work): the answers researchers need "lie at lower levels of granularity: the level of theoretical and empirical claims or statements made within publications," and multiple opposing claims can coexist because "each claim is linked to the underlying evidence" so readers "assess the validity of each claim on its own merit." The protocol runs on backlink-capable clients (Roam, Obsidian, Logseq). Transfer: when Softland imports a Discourse Graph project, the topology view should preserve and display node *types* and relation *types* — and the claim/evidence/question distinction is itself a model for Softland's "accepted facts vs. candidates" visual encoding.

**Notion / Coda — databases-as-views.** Notion lets the same database appear as table, board, timeline, calendar, gallery, or list; "switching views does not change your database items, only how they appear… If you edit a date in a calendar view, that date updates in table, board, and every other view," and every entry is itself a page. The API treats views as first-class objects scoped to one data source with their own filters/sorts/layout. Rationale: one source of truth, many task-shaped projections. Transfer: this is the consumer-grade proof of Softland's Projection/View principle — implement views as configuration over shared ObjectContainers.

**Linear — dense, keyboard-first, minimal-chrome design for power users.** Linear's design (dense lists, command palette, saved views, status grouping/swimlanes) optimizes for speed and recognition over decoration. Rationale: power users value information density and keyboard velocity once oriented. Transfer: Softland's source inventory and object browser should favor dense, scannable lists with keyboard navigation, not sparse cards.

### Cross-cutting answers

- **Accepted vs. candidate encoding:** Discourse Graphs (typed nodes), Figma (solid vs. dashed selection box; diamond instance icon), and DataHub (health badges) all show that *categorical status should be encoded redundantly* — shape + color + label, never color alone (this also satisfies color-blind accessibility). Softland must render accepted CompositionEdges as solid/definite and any future candidate connections as visually distinct (dashed, muted, separated into their own region) so truth is never confused with guess.
- **Derived↔raw mapping affordances:** source maps and VS Code Peek both show the trustworthy pattern is *exact, reversible, low-cost* reveal of origin. SourceAnchor inspection should open the precise raw span inline.
- **Useful graph vs. hairball:** local scoping (Obsidian depth slider), one-hop expansion (DataHub), degree-of-interest filtering (Furnas), and edge bundling/cutting (the "Grooming/Trimming the hairball" literature) are the proven techniques. Default to local + depth-limited + status-filtered.
- **Three-pane earns its keep** when it maps to distinct cognitive jobs (browse / focus / inspect) and is selection-driven (Figma, VS Code, IDEs); it fails when panes compete for the same job or when the inspector is empty most of the time.
- **What's never hidden vs. folded:** governed by information scent (Pirolli/Card), progressive disclosure, recognition-over-recall, and Furnas DOI. Never hide: provenance path to source, object identity, accepted-vs-candidate status, error/partial-import status. Safe to fold: full raw text bodies, low-DOI distant neighbors, revision history details, secondary metadata.
- **Orientation surfaces:** breadcrumbs, "you are here" highlights, minimaps and overviews reduce disorientation by externalizing the user's location in the structure — the same reason Engelbart's outline view and map-style overviews exist.

### Mapping to the 18 deliverables (condensed)
1. *Product interpretation:* Softland's first view is an **orientation instrument over imported terrain** — a programmable epistemic interface in read-only mode.
2. *Design principles:* orientation-before-manipulation; provenance always inspectable; raw+native both present; accepted≠candidate; local-over-global; views-as-projections; identity-preserving semantic zoom; degree-of-interest folding.
3. *Information architecture:* Silo → Source → ObjectContainer → DerivedUnit/span, with SourceAnchors and CompositionEdges as traversable relations; cross-source accepted connections as a separate layer.
4. *First screen:* three-pane (inventory / topology browser / inspector) + optional bottom connections-and-islands strip; Shneiderman overview default.
5. *Source/silo inventory (left):* dense list grouped by silo with counts, status, freshness, errors (DataHub catalog + Linear density).
6. *Object/topology browser (center):* mode switch list / outline / local-graph / timeline; default list/outline; graph is local + depth-limited (Obsidian/DataHub).
7. *Inspector (right):* selection-driven, Figma-style; tabs for raw source, native representation, revisions, anchors, composition edges, incoming/outgoing connections.
8. *Raw vs. native:* side-by-side or toggle with exact SourceAnchor reveal (source maps); native is labeled as derived-from.
9. *Local graph:* one-hop expansion, depth slider, incoming/outgoing distinction, status badges; never global.
10. *Timeline/history:* revisions and import/composition events along time (PROV activities); a ViewSpec/projection, not a separate copy.
11. *Empty/loading/error:* explicit partial-import, unresolved-anchor, and disconnected-island states.
12. *Interaction model:* Peek-style inspect-without-leaving as default; explicit jump for committed navigation; keyboard-first.
13. *Clickable:* every source, object, anchor, edge, connection, silo; every count expands.
14. *Never hidden:* provenance path, identity, accepted/candidate status, error/partial status.
15. *Folded/compressed:* raw bodies, distant low-DOI nodes, revision detail, secondary metadata — recoverable on demand.
16. *Visual references:* source maps, VS Code Peek, DataHub lineage, Figma triad, Obsidian local graph, Notion views, Linear density.
17. *Anti-patterns:* global hairball graph; color-only status encoding; context-destroying jumps; copies-instead-of-projections; hidden provenance; ambiguous edge-arrow direction.
18. *Kernel assumptions:* stable ObjectContainer identity across revisions; SourceArtifacts preserved and addressable to exact spans; SourceAnchors exact and reversible; CompositionEdges carry type/order; Projection/View layer can query without copying; accepted vs. candidate status is a first-class field.

### Applying the two grounding examples
- **Softland project (markdown, code, transcripts, commits):** left inventory groups four silos with per-silo counts and freshness; selecting `design-notes.md` populates the center outline (headings → blocks as DerivedUnits) and the right inspector shows raw markdown beside the native object, its SourceAnchors, the CompositionEdges to child blocks, and an accepted cross-source edge to the commit that references it. The local graph at depth 1 shows the doc, its blocks, and the linked commit — not the whole repo.
- **Discourse Graph project (Roam, codebase, Linear, transcripts):** the inventory surfaces the Roam silo with Question/Claim/Evidence node-type counts; the browser preserves node types as visual categories; an Evidence node's inspector shows its raw Roam block via SourceAnchor, its *supports*/*opposes* edges (typed, solid for accepted), and any candidate connections to Linear issues kept in a visually separated region.

## Recommendations
1. **Build the three-pane orientation shell first**, defaulting the center to list/outline (not graph), with Shneiderman's mantra as the explicit interaction contract. *Change this only if* user testing shows people enter looking for a specific known object — then lead with search (DataHub's search-first catalog model).
2. **Implement SourceAnchor reveal as the trust anchor of the whole product**, copying the source-map/Peek pattern: exact, inline, reversible, one keystroke. This is the single highest-leverage feature for the "provenance must remain inspectable" principle.
3. **Make the graph local-only from day one** — depth slider, one-hop expansion, status badges, incoming/outgoing split. *Threshold to revisit:* Obsidian's community-observed legibility limits (clean under ~50 nodes, degrading past ~200) suggest adding degree-of-interest filtering and edge bundling before allowing deeper defaults once a depth-1 neighborhood routinely exceeds ~50 nodes; note that link *density* matters as much as raw node count.
4. **Encode accepted vs. candidate redundantly** (shape + fill + label + spatial separation) and keep candidate/future connections in their own region so the read-only "truth" layer is never visually contaminated.
5. **Treat every view as a projection over the kernel's ObjectContainers**, validating with the two grounding examples (Softland project; Discourse Graph project) that switching list↔outline↔graph↔timeline never duplicates or loses object identity.

## Caveats
- Several lineage sources are visionary/aspirational (Xanadu was famously never fully shipped — Wired called it "the longest-running vaporware story"; Dynamicland is an active research lab, not a product), so their *rationale* transfers more reliably than their implementations.
- The "global graphs are useless hairballs" claim is well-supported by practitioner consensus and the hairball research literature, but the node-count thresholds cited (≈50 / 200 / 500) come from community observation (r/ObsidianMD via Code Culture), not a controlled study; set Softland's own thresholds by testing, accounting for link density.
- PROV-style provenance notations carry a documented usability risk (arrow-direction misreading); adopt the *semantics* but design the *visuals* fresh with plain-verb edge labels.
- The original Reenskaug MVC differs from the Smalltalk-80 implementation (Althoff et al., released 1983); cite the *principle* of one-model-many-views, which both share, rather than either specific controller mechanics.
- Production-tool details (Figma's panel behavior, Notion's view API, DataHub's expansion rules) reflect current implementations and evolve; verify against live docs before committing pixel-level specs.
- This report deliberately scopes to the read-only first view; editing, candidate acceptance, semantic search, and LLM continuation are out of scope per the task and should not be retrofitted into these recommendations without revisiting the principles.

# Designing the Imported Topology View for Softland

## Softland as epistemic place

In design terms, Softland should be treated as an **environment for entering, re-entering, and handing off understanding**, not as a container for files. The closest historical lineage is not generic productivity software; it is Bush’s Memex with its associative trails through records, Engelbart’s framing of computing as a way to improve comprehension in complex problem situations, Dynamicland’s idea of a computer that is a place, and Ink & Switch’s tools-for-thought tradition of helping people think, collaborate, and keep track of history across media. Those references all point toward a product that makes structure, lineage, and context inhabitable, not merely searchable. citeturn15view0turn15view2turn21view0turn16view0turn16view1turn16view3

That framing matters because the Imported Topology View is the **front porch of the world**, not the whole world. Its job is to answer, quickly and credibly, what came in, what was created, how to get back to source, what is already related, and where the gaps are. The right analogies are VS Code’s explorer, breadcrumbs, outline, and timeline; Figma’s left navigation plus right properties panel; Chrome DevTools’ authored-versus-deployed mapping; and lineage tools such as DataHub and dbt that keep origin, downstream structure, and warnings visible without forcing the user into a giant global graph. citeturn1view0turn1view1turn11view2turn1view2turn1view3turn11view1turn18view0turn10view4turn17view0

The strongest product interpretation, then, is this: **Softland is a place made of durable identities, visible trails, and recoverable compression**. The Imported Topology View should therefore behave like a scoped terrain view. It should give an overview first, let the user zoom and filter into a local region, and reveal details on demand. It should also preserve identity across scale, in the same spirit as semantic zooming: when something gets smaller, it should become a different representation of the same object, not a lossy copy or a disappearing node. citeturn1view0turn11view0turn1view4

## Principles for imported topology

The first principle should be **orientation before manipulation**. Shneiderman’s information-seeking mantra remains the right baseline: begin with an overview, then allow zooming and filtering, then reveal details. Applied to Softland, that means the opening screen should not ask “what do you want to do?” but “where am I, what exists here, what is connected, and what looks questionable?” A stable overview should stay visible while inspection deepens. citeturn1view0

The second principle should be **provenance by construction**. Provenance research in visualization distinguishes between histories of data, computation, interaction, and insight; for a read-only imported view, the minimum trustworthy chain is: source artifact → exact anchor → native object or derived unit → accepted relations → revision/history. Chrome DevTools is a useful operational precedent because it keeps original and transformed code visible together and surfaces mapping failures explicitly, instead of pretending the transformation is seamless. citeturn10view0turn11view1turn18view0

The third principle should be **raw source and Softland-native form must coexist**. A user should never have to choose between “where did this come from?” and “what did Softland make of it?” DevTools source maps are the clearest analog: the executed artifact and the authored artifact are distinct, but the interface lets a person move continuously between them. Softland should do the same for imported markdown, chat transcripts, Roam blocks, code files, issues, and future source types. citeturn11view1turn18view0

The fourth principle should be **accepted truth must be visually distinct from uncertainty**. Uncertainty-visualization research repeatedly notes that computer interfaces tend to make information look more absolute than it really is, and that exposing uncertainty improves understanding and communication. In Softland, accepted cross-source links, exact anchors, and established object identities should therefore be rendered as stable truth. Candidate relations, partial parses, stale anchors, import warnings, and incomplete lineages should live in a different visual lane and should never silently merge into “already true.” dbt’s lineage warnings and Chrome’s source-map status/error tables are good precedents for keeping this visible. citeturn10view1turn10view2turn17view0turn18view0

The fifth principle should be **local context over world graph spectacle**. Obsidian’s local graph is useful precisely because it scopes attention to notes around the active note and exposes depth control, while DataHub explicitly limits some lineage expansion patterns to keep the visualization simple. Softland should follow that lead: default to the neighborhood of the selected scope or object, and treat all-world graph views as an anti-pattern for this first release. citeturn1view4turn10view4

The sixth principle should be **views are projections, not copies**. Your brief already fixes this at the kernel level, and the UI should make that legible: the left inventory, center browser, inspector, local graph, and timeline should all be synchronized lenses over the same substrate. That is also how the strongest reference products behave: VS Code’s outline and breadcrumbs are alternate projections over the same file/symbol structure; Figma’s layers and properties panels are synchronized projections over the same selected layer; Linear’s filters and custom views are durable filtered projections over the same issues. citeturn1view1turn11view2turn1view2turn1view3turn11view3turn11view4

## Information architecture of the view

The information architecture should make six layers visible on the first screen, in this order of abstraction: **silos**, **source artifacts**, **native objects**, **anchors**, **accepted relations**, and **exceptions**. “Exceptions” is important: disconnected islands, unanchored objects, partial imports, stale anchors, and unresolved candidate relations should appear as first-class topology, not as hidden log output. DevTools’ explicit status/error handling and dbt’s explicit lineage caveats are strong evidence that trust rises when failure states are surfaced in the same interface as the successful structure. citeturn18view0turn17view0

The opening questions from your brief map naturally onto that IA. “What did we import?” is answered at the silo and source-artifact layers. “What native objects were created?” is answered at the native-object layer. “How are they grounded?” is answered at the anchor layer. “What relationships already exist?” is answered at the accepted-relations layer. “What is disconnected or unresolved?” is answered at the exceptions layer. This is why the screen should not lead with vanity metrics; it should lead with a **scoped explanatory inventory**. That is closer to an explorer, outline, and lineage browser than to a dashboard. citeturn1view1turn11view2turn10view4

For the **Softland project** example, the visible silos would likely be markdown docs, code files, chat transcripts, and commits/history. Within those, source artifacts would include individual `.md` files, code files, transcript files, and commit streams. Native objects might include imported documents, heading-derived containers, code-level objects, or object containers representing stable entities. Anchors would point to exact file ranges, transcript turns, or commit positions. Accepted relations might connect a design doc section to a transcript decision and then to code touched by later commits. Disconnected islands would reveal material that came in but has not yet been bridged to the rest of the terrain.

For the **Discourse Graph project** example, the silos would likely be Roam graph data, the codebase, Linear issues, and chat threads. A selected Roam page should reveal native objects and anchors to specific blocks; a selected Linear issue should reveal whether it already connects to code artifacts, design notes, or transcript evidence; and the “exceptions” layer should make it obvious which issues, pages, or chat clusters remain isolated. In both examples, the same IA supports orientation without requiring a universal graph.

## The first screen

The best first-screen structure is a **three-pane orientation layout** with an optional bottom tray. This is the most credible synthesis of the relevant patterns: VS Code shows that explorer, outline, breadcrumbs, and timeline can coexist without feeling like business analytics; Figma shows that a left navigation surface plus a persistent right properties panel works especially well in view-only inspection modes; and Linear shows how dense filtering can remain legible when it is attached to a current scope rather than the whole world. citeturn1view1turn11view2turn1view2turn1view3turn11view3turn11view4

```text
┌──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┐
│ Source / Silo        │ Imported Topology Browser                   │ Inspector                   │
│ Inventory            │                                              │                             │
│                      │ Breadcrumbs: Silo / Artifact / Object        │ Selected identity           │
│ Silos                │ Scope chips: Source • Object type • Status   │ Type • Stable ID • Status   │
│ • Markdown           │ View: Outline | Neighborhood | Timeline      │                             │
│ • Transcripts        │                                              │ Raw source                  │
│ • Code               │ Selected scope summary                       │ Native representation       │
│ • Roam / DG          │ 24 artifacts • 163 objects • 412 anchors     │ Anchors                     │
│ • Linear             │ 18 accepted cross-source links • 5 islands   │ Composition                 │
│ • History            │                                              │ Incoming / outgoing links   │
│                      │ Outline / list / local graph / timeline      │ Revisions / history         │
│ Status               │ for the current scope                        │                             │
│ • OK                 │                                              │ Warnings / unresolved       │
│ • Partial            │                                              │                             │
│ • Error              │                                              │                             │
└──────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────┘

Optional bottom tray: Accepted cross-source connections | Disconnected islands | Candidate relations
```

The **left pane** should be the Source/Silo Inventory. It should group imported material by source family and then allow expansion into source artifacts. Each row should show counts that help with legibility rather than productivity theater: artifacts imported, native objects created, anchors resolved, accepted cross-source links present, disconnected count, freshness, and status. Freshness and status matter because the user is orienting to the imported terrain, and lineage/debugging tools consistently make status and last-known history visible at the point of navigation. citeturn18view0turn11view2turn10view4

The **center pane** should be the Object/Topology Browser, and its default mode should be **Outline**, not Graph. VS Code’s outline is a better precedent than a graph canvas for first-pass understanding because imported material is often structurally hierarchical before it is relationally global. A selected markdown file wants headings and contained objects; a selected transcript wants turns, segments, and derived units; a selected issue wants comments, linked artifacts, and descendants. Graph mode belongs here as a **local neighborhood mode**, not as the homepage. citeturn1view1turn11view2turn1view4

The **right pane** should be a persistent Inspector. Figma’s view-only properties panel is the right reference: selection on the left or canvas should always update the right-side inspector, and the inspector should remain stable enough that users build place-memory around it. In Softland, that panel should prioritize identity, truth status, raw/native duality, anchors, relations, and history before any decorative preview. citeturn1view3turn1view2

The **optional bottom tray** should be present, but not dominant. It should host accepted cross-source connections, disconnected islands, and candidate relations as three separate tabs or lanes. Accepted connections can be shown in the main scope summary, but candidates should remain subordinate and visually distinct. This layout keeps the main frame trustworthy while still exposing what remains unresolved. citeturn10view1turn10view2turn17view0

Visually, the screen should be **dense, quiet, and explanatory**. Distill is a useful tonal reference for serious, web-native explanation; VS Code and Linear are useful references for dense but low-noise information surfaces. What to avoid is the polished emptiness of a marketing dashboard: large KPI cards, gradient hero space, oversized charts, and decorative motion that competes with actual epistemic structure. citeturn16view4turn11view2turn11view3

## Inspection surfaces

The **Source/Silo Inventory** should function like a map legend plus import ledger. A silo row should show what family of material exists and whether that family imported cleanly. Expanding a silo should reveal source artifacts with stable labels, import timestamps, freshness, and warning counts. Unsupported or partially interpreted sources should still appear here as legitimate terrain; the point is to say “this exists, but Softland has only partially metabolized it,” not to hide it because it does not yet fit cleanly into the native substrate. DevTools’ explicit map-load failures and dbt’s lineage caveats are exactly the right behavioral precedent. citeturn18view0turn17view0

The **Object/Topology Browser** should support three modes in its header: **Outline**, **Neighborhood**, and **Timeline**. Outline should be default because it is the most legible compression for hierarchies and composition edges. Neighborhood should show a local graph centered on the current object or scope. Timeline should show the history relevant to that scope. Filtering should be scoped and plainspoken: source type, object type, anchored/unanchored, connected/disconnected, accepted-only, warnings, and maybe a simple text filter over the current scope. This is closer to VS Code tree filtering and Linear filtering than to semantic search, and it stays inside the product boundary you set. citeturn11view2turn11view3

Each row in the browser should have enough information for trust at a glance: title, type, stable identity hint, source badge, anchor state, accepted-link count, child count, and warning badge. Errors and warnings should be visible in the list itself, the same way VS Code’s outline can surface problems at a glance. That matters because users should be able to scan for weak spots in interpretation without opening every node. citeturn1view1turn11view2

The **Selected-Object Inspector** should have a fixed internal order. First, an identity card: object name, type, stable ID, source count, revision count, truth state, and current scope path. Second, a dual representation area: raw source and Softland-native representation. Third, anchors. Fourth, relations. Fifth, revisions/history. Sixth, warnings. This ordering matches the user’s likely trust-building sequence: what is this, where is it from, how exactly is it grounded, what else is it tied to, and what changed over time. citeturn1view3turn10view0turn11view1

The **raw-source versus native-representation** design should be explicit and paired. The cleanest implementation is a split panel inside the inspector: on one side, a source excerpt with exact highlighted span, source location labels, and “reveal in source” affordance; on the other side, the Softland-native object card with fields, containment path, revision pointer, and “reveal neighbors” affordance. If the selection is a DerivedUnit without stable native identity, the interface should say so directly. If an object has multiple anchors, the source side should expose them as a list rather than pretending there is one canonical source location. DevTools source maps are the best reference for this exact authored/native duality. citeturn11view1turn18view0

The **local graph or neighborhood view** should be tightly scoped: selected node in the center, immediate neighbors grouped by edge type, optional second-hop expansion, and a clear depth control. Obsidian’s local graph and depth slider are the simplest precedent; dbt’s column-level lineage and DataHub’s focused lineage views are useful for showing how smaller, typed neighborhoods can be more valuable than a universal map. In Softland, graph mode should emphasize typed relations such as contains, ordered-within, anchored-to, derived-from, and accepted-cross-source-related-to. Composition edges should still be better represented in outline form than as free-floating nodes. citeturn1view4turn10view4turn17view0

The **timeline/history/provenance view** should be unified but filterable. VS Code’s timeline is a good precedent because it can show commits and local changes in one place while still letting the user filter sources. Softland should do the same conceptually: source timestamps, import timestamps, object revisions, commit history if imported, and accepted-relation establishment events should appear in a single ordered stream for the selected scope. Shneiderman’s taxonomy explicitly treats “history” as one of the core tasks of information visualization, so this is not accessory UI; it is part of orientation. citeturn11view2turn6search0turn1view0

## Interaction model and states

The interaction model should be **selection-centric and scope-preserving**. Clicking a silo sets the scope. Clicking a source artifact narrows the browser to that artifact. Clicking an object selects it and populates the inspector. Clicking an anchor reveals the exact raw-source span. Clicking a relation pivots the browser into a local neighborhood around that edge or target. Breadcrumbs should always permit stepping back up through the containing path, and the interface should preserve local navigation history so a user can backtrack through an inspection trail the way they do in an IDE. citeturn1view1turn11view2turn11view3

The disclosure rules should be strict because the entire point of this screen is trust.

| Must be clickable | Must never be hidden | Should stay folded unless requested |
|---|---|---|
| Every silo row | Stable object identity and type | Full raw documents outside the anchored excerpt |
| Every source artifact row | Source origin and anchor presence | Full descendant trees beyond the current local scope |
| Every native object row | Accepted vs candidate vs warning state | Candidate relation details |
| Every anchor and source-location badge | Containing path / breadcrumb context | Repetitive metadata fields |
| Every relation badge and disconnected-island row | Import failures, stale anchors, unresolved status | Far-hop global graph expansion |
| Every timeline event and warning badge | Counts for disconnected / unanchored / partial items in current scope | Secondary historical detail not relevant to the current selection |

The product should be explicit about **empty, loading, partial, and error states**. A blank workspace should explain that Imported Topology appears after sources are imported and transformed into source artifacts and native objects. Loading should be staged, not spinner-only: “loading source artifacts,” then “loading native objects,” then “resolving anchors,” then “loading accepted relations.” Partial imports should remain browseable and should surface exact failures in the same place the successful structure appears. This mirrors how DevTools exposes statuses and errors for source maps and how dbt exposes incomplete lineage and warnings inside the lineage UI itself. citeturn18view0turn17view0

A serious epistemic workspace should also support **keyboard-first reading and inspection**. Tree navigation, expand/collapse, filter focus, next/previous warning, next/previous disconnected island, and quick reveal-in-source are more important here than gestural canvas manipulation. The visual treatment should reinforce that: compact rows, disciplined typography, restrained color, distinctive icons for object/source/relation classes, and color reserved primarily for state and warnings. That is the information-density lesson from VS Code and Linear, while Distill is the reminder that clarity and vividness should come from explanation, not ornament. citeturn11view2turn11view3turn16view4

## Patterns to borrow, anti-patterns to avoid, and kernel assumptions

The most useful references to borrow are not whole products but **specific interaction contracts**. From VS Code: explorer, breadcrumbs, outline, timeline, and list-integrated warnings. From Figma: left navigation plus persistent right inspector in a view-only mode. From Chrome DevTools: explicit separation between authored and transformed representations, plus visible status/error for broken mappings. From Obsidian: local graph around the active node. From DataHub and dbt: focused lineage, warnings, impact-oriented local expansion, and the ability to inspect a single column or entity rather than the entire universe. From Linear: dense scoped filters and durable views. From Pad++: semantic zoom as different representations of the same object at different scales. From Distill and Dynamicland: the broader sensibility that understanding should be clear, vivid, spatially legible, and publicly inspectable. citeturn11view2turn1view2turn1view3turn11view1turn18view0turn1view4turn10view4turn17view0turn11view3turn11view4turn11view0turn16view4turn16view1

The anti-patterns are correspondingly sharp. Do **not** open on a giant force-directed graph. Do **not** replace topology with KPI cards. Do **not** flatten everything into a generic file manager. Do **not** hide provenance behind secondary modals. Do **not** merge candidate relations with accepted edges. Do **not** let views create the impression that there are separate copies of the same object. Obsidian’s local graph, DataHub’s constrained expansion, and uncertainty/provenance research all push toward the same lesson: clarity comes from scoped context, typed relations, and visible grounds for trust, not from maximal simultaneous display. citeturn1view4turn10view4turn10view0turn10view1turn10view2

The Imported Topology View also depends on a few kernel assumptions. These are not new kernel designs, but they are the minimum contracts the UI needs in order to work:

| Kernel assumption | Why the view needs it |
|---|---|
| Stable IDs for `SourceArtifact`, `ObjectContainer`, `Revision`, and `DerivedUnit` | So selection, breadcrumbs, links, and history remain durable across views |
| Exact `SourceAnchor` resolution with status | So raw-source inspection can highlight precise spans and report stale or failed mappings |
| Typed `CompositionEdge` and accepted relation edge metadata | So outline, neighborhood, and relation lists can distinguish containment from cross-source linkage |
| Clear accepted vs candidate relation state | So truth and uncertainty can be rendered differently |
| Queryable scoped neighborhoods with counts first | So the UI can show local topology without loading a giant all-world graph |
| Revision/event history with source time and import time | So the timeline can distinguish source chronology from Softland chronology |
| Disconnected-component and orphan detection | So unresolved islands can be treated as first-class topology |
| Human-readable labels and type metadata per object | So explorer rows and inspector cards are legible without expensive interpretation in the client |
| Deterministic path information for containment | So breadcrumbs and reveal-in-context interactions always work |
| Projection-safe identity across view modes | So outline, graph, timeline, and inspector all feel like different projections over one world |

If this view is done well, the user’s first experience of imported material will feel like arriving somewhere intelligible. They will not see “a bunch of ingested stuff.” They will see terrain: silos, paths, anchor points, neighborhoods, cross-links, history, and unresolved edges. That is the right first move for a product whose ambition is to make understanding inhabitable.
